title: Prototyping in code, not in Figma specs
subtitle: At Bibel TV I stopped handing engineering static specs and started handing them working code
team: Design-led, with an engineering partner. Hamburg / Berlin

sections.headline: Prototyping in code, not in Figma specs
sections.subtext: The usual handoff treats design and engineering as two steps in a line. At Bibel TV I closed the gap: I prototyped in real code with real APIs, and engineering built on the prototype directly. No redline specs in between.

sections.quote: The prototype is not a mockup. It is the first working version of the product.
sections.context: The shift in what a design prototype is for

sections.headline: The handoff problem
sections.content:
The standard process runs in sequence. A designer works in Figma, writes specs, redlines measurements and states. Engineering builds from the document. Design reviews the build, finds the gaps, and the two sides go back and forth for weeks.

Every handoff in that chain loses information. A spec can say a card should feel premium; it cannot say what that means in padding, contrast, and motion. And the code engineering writes from a spec has no connection to the thinking that produced the design.

sections.headline: What I do instead
sections.content:
At Bibel TV I design the concept in Figma, layout, flow, hierarchy, and then prototype it in real code, using AI-assisted coding tools to move quickly. The prototype runs on the actual Bibel TV APIs, with real videos and real metadata.

Engineering does not receive a spec. They receive a working prototype, and they build on its component structures, API calls, and navigation patterns. They refine; they do not re-implement. When a technical constraint shows up, I change the prototype in code, in the same medium as the product. There is no handoff step to lose anything in.

steps.label: Concept in Figma
steps.description: I still start in Figma for layout, flow, and visual hierarchy. That defines the intent, the what.

steps.label: Prototype in real code
steps.description: I build the prototype in code with AI-assisted tools, against the real Bibel TV APIs. Design decisions get made in the working medium: layouts, interactions, edge cases.

steps.label: Real data, not placeholders
steps.description: The prototype runs on actual content: real videos, real metadata. That surfaces problems placeholder data never shows.

steps.label: Engineering builds on it
steps.description: Engineering reviews the prototype code and reuses its structure directly. Refinement, not re-implementation.

sections.headline: A real example: the Android gradients
sections.content:
I built the web prototype first, with gradients that looked good in the browser. Moving to Android, the gradient rendering raised real quality concerns, visible banding, and performance questions on lower-end devices.

The old way: file a ticket, explain the problem to engineering, wait for an assessment, maybe redesign. Instead, I iterated on the Android prototype in code, tested alternatives against real rendering, and found one that held up. Engineering got a working reference, not a problem report.

sections.headline: What changed

metrics.label: Iteration speed
metrics.before: A design change took 3–5 days through the spec-and-handoff cycle
metrics.after: Hours: change it, run it on real data, judge it in the same session

metrics.label: What engineering received
metrics.before: Figma specs and redlines to interpret
metrics.after: Working prototype code, reused directly in the build

metrics.label: Platform decisions
metrics.value: Web-first assumptions were corrected on the Android prototype, before production work started

sections.narrative: A web-first assumption got caught and corrected on the Android prototype before a line of production code was written. The cultural change was harder than the technical one: it took trust for engineering to treat prototype code as a real design artifact. Once the first prototype became production code, that trust came on its own.

sections.headline: What I took from it
sections.content:
Working code is the clearest design spec because it removes ambiguity. When engineering reviews a running prototype, they see exactly what works and exactly what does not.

This way of working asks for a design leader who is comfortable in code, not writing production systems, but building prototypes that carry intent. It is worth the stretch. When the prototype is working code, the design-to-ship gap mostly disappears.

executive.summary: Closed the design-to-ship gap at Bibel TV by prototyping in real code with real APIs. Engineering builds on the prototype directly. Iteration dropped from days to hours.
executive.angle: Design leadership through a faster design-engineering loop

blog.summary: Figma-spec-then-handoff has a faster alternative: prototype in code, iterate with engineering, and let the prototype become the product. Here is how it worked at Bibel TV.
blog.angle: Making prototype code a real design artifact
